First public allegation: Swedish Radio, 16 Apr 1987 [reported]
Investigating body: CBI (FIR 22 Jan 1990, RC 1(A)/90; chargesheet 22 Oct 1999) [documented]

Latest stage: all proceedings quashed/discharged (Delhi HC 4 Feb 2004 in part; 31 May 2005 fully for the Hinduja brothers and the Bofors company) [documented]; SC dismissed CBI's SLP 2 Nov 2018 for a 4,522-day delay (limitation, not merits) [reported]; SC dismissed the last pending appeal, filed by an advocate, 6 Aug 2026 [documented: three outlets]
Counter-record: the 2005 judgment records that the investigation ran 14 years and cost nearly Rs 250 crore and calls the case a bubble that 'burst'; no conviction in the case [documented]
Case record fields: subject; decision-date and government at the time; first public allegation; investigating body; latest stage; counter-record.

Record (dated): contract 1986-03-24, about ₹1,437.72 crore (CMM order); Swedish Radio allegation 1987-04-16; Swiss banks released about 500 documents in 1997 after litigation; Delhi HC 2004-02-04 quashed charges and held the late Prime Minister (1984–89) entitled to be seen as innocent since no trial was possible; Delhi HC 2005-05-31 discharged the Hinduja brothers; Delhi court 2011-03-04 allowed CBI to close the case against the Italian agent, who died 2013-07-12; Supreme Court 2026-08-06 dismissed the final plea [documented for 2004 (judgment opened); reported for the rest (Wikipedia)]

What the record establishes: payments to agents from Bofors were documented in Swiss accounts; receipt by any Indian public servant was never established in any court; the investigation ran 13 years to the 2004 judgment and the matter 39 years to 2026 without a conviction [analytic]

claims.d: Three donors with a defence or strategic-works line (Megha Engineering Rs 966 cr, Mahindra & Mahindra Rs 25 cr, Cyient Rs 10 cr; total Rs 1,001 cr, 8.2% of all matched bonds) gave Rs 619 cr to the BJP (61.8% of their total) against 47.6% (value-weighted) for all 224 donors of Rs 10 crore or more and 46.1% of all matched bonds (Rs 5,594.20 cr of Rs 12,145.88 cr). Megha is 96.5% of the pool, and its only strategic work in this file before 2023 is an NHIDCL (MoRTH) award with no MoD award; a MEIL group company (ICOMM Tele Ltd) signed a ~Rs 500 cr MoD contract on 15 Jun 2023 (see narrative 0). The Mahindra bond was bought by the listed parent, not by the subsidiary that holds the 2021 MoD contract. Like-for-like counts: 2 of the 3 gave only to the BJP and 3 of 3 gave to it at least once, against 86 of 224 (38.4%) and 165 of 224 (73.7%) among all donors of Rs 10 crore or more; across all 1,280 normalised donor names, 372 (29.1%) gave only to the BJP and 519 (40.5%) at least once. Infrastructure control (same table, re-read 2026-10-06): NCC Rs 60/60 cr, Navayuga Engineering 55/55, APCO Infratech 30/30, KEC International 11/11 and Kalpataru Projects 25.5/25.5 to the BJP; Jindal Steel & Power 3/123. Megha also gave Rs 382 cr to eight other parties (BRS 195, DMK 85, YSRCP 37, TDP 28, Congress 18, JD(U) 10, JD(S) 5, Janasena 4). Window: the matched set covers purchases from Apr 2019 to Feb 2024, not the whole scheme from 2018. Responses: the donors were not asked; the BJP's public answer on bonds (the verdict cites Amit Shah, 15 Mar 2024) was not opened here. The names Tata, L&T, Bharat Forge/Kalyani, Solar Industries, Zen Technologies, Hikvision/Prama and Adani do not appear as donors in the ADR list.

claims.lab: CCS (Pension) Amendment Rules 2021 (G.S.R. 360(E), 31 May 2021): no publication without clearance by retirees of intelligence and security organisations
claims.d: G.S.R. 360(E) of 31 May 2021 substituted clause (a) of Rule 8(3A) of the CCS (Pension) Rules 1972 and Form 26: no Government servant who worked in an intelligence or security-related organisation in the Second Schedule of the RTI Act 'shall, without prior clearance from the Head of the Organisation, make any publication after retirement' of material on the organisation's domain, personnel or expertise; the Head of the Organisation decides what is sensitive; loss of pension rights is the sanction. ORF counts 26 organisations, including IB, R&AW, DRI, CBI, NCB, BSF, CRPF, ITBP and CISF. Because the notification substitutes an existing clause (a), it widens an earlier restriction rather than creating a new one; the earlier clause's text (UPA-era, approval by the Head of Department) was not opened. It does not amend the Army Rules, and the brief's '2021 amendment to the Army Rules on public comment' was not found; retired armed forces personnel and ED officials are not covered. In the consolidated CCS (Pension) Rules 2021 (G.S.R. 868(E), 20 Dec 2021) the provision is Rule 7(4)(a).

Rafale (36-aircraft purchase announced 10 Apr 2015; contract signed 23 Sep 2016, BJP government): first public allegation 24 Sep 2016 (Congress, price), the Reliance/HAL allegation in Nov 2017, the Hollande remark via Mediapart 21 Sep 2018 [reported: Wikipedia]; no investigation ordered by the Supreme Court, which dismissed the petitions (2018) and the review (2019); a French judicial inquiry was opened on 14 Jun 2021 (ThePrint; status unknown); CAG Report 3 of 2019 (2.86% below the audit-aligned price; price redacted); convictions: 0. Common feature: an allegation about an intermediary (Bofors 1987; Rafale, Mediapart Nov 2021, not opened here) or an offset partner (Rafale 2017–18), each denied by the government of the day — in Bofors the then Prime Minister told the Lok Sabha on 20 Apr 1987 that no middlemen were involved (as recorded in press timelines; debate not opened); in Rafale the Ministry said it had no role in choosing the offset partner (c064).
claims.innocentReading: The two cases differ in kind: Bofors was a contract with alleged commissions through intermediaries and a criminal chargesheet; Rafale is a government-to-government deal reviewed on petition, with no investigation ordered. Different eras, different statutes (s.17A of the Prevention of Corruption Act since 2018) and an open court file in one, a redacted one in the other.

The Tatra column merges two proceedings (the BEML/intermediary FIR and the PC Act bribe-offer trial). In both, the then Defence Minister referred the matter to the CBI after the first public allegation (the Italian arrest of Feb 2013; the Army Chief's 2012 disclosure), and both involve an intermediary and a retired senior officer in the record (a former Air Chief; a retired Lt Gen).
claims.innocentReading: Chargesheets and framed charges are allegations tested slowly; the absence of a conviction after 7–13 years reflects court delay as much as weakness of evidence, and the Italian acquittals are the only completed trials. A near-100% no-conviction base rate across defence cases makes 'convictions 0' non-discriminating between the two.

claims.lab: Cases by government at first allegation or FIR: UPA beside NDA, same fields
claims.d: Keyed by the government at the first allegation or FIR, not the decision date. Under UPA (2004–14): AgustaWestland (contract 2010; FIR 2013), Tatra (purchases since 1986; FIR 2012), Sukna (NOC 2009; court of inquiry 2009–10), Adarsh (allotment and clearances in the 2000s, mostly by the Maharashtra government, overlapping NDA-I at the Centre; CBI FIR 2011). Under NDA (2014–): Rafale (contract 2016; first allegation 2016), Pegasus (alleged purchase reported for 2017; first allegation 2021). Bofors (1986) predates both. FIR or disciplinary proceeding opened by the government of the day: UPA column 4 of 4 (CBI FIRs in AgustaWestland, Tatra and Adarsh, ordered by UPA's own ministers; an Army court of inquiry and court martial in Sukna), all continued under NDA; NDA column 0 of 2 (Rafale: none in India; Pegasus: a Supreme Court-appointed technical committee, not a government inquiry). Latest stage of the seven: quashed/discharged (Bofors); petitions dismissed in India, French judicial inquiry opened 2021 (Rafale); Italian acquittals and Indian trial at pre-charge stage (AgustaWestland); CBI closure report and a separate trial (Tatra); demolition stayed, sanction quashed, appeals pending (Adarsh); court-martial outcomes set aside — AFT acquittal on merits 5 Sep 2014 (c084) and SC set-aside on GCM composition 24 Jan 2019 (c085) (Sukna); inconclusive, report sealed (Pegasus). Sukna, Adarsh and Pegasus are not procurement cases. Final convictions in the records opened: 0 of 7. The count is of the seven cases the brief names, not a sample of defence procurement.
claims.innocentReading: Seven hand-picked cases cannot rank two governments: they are the cases that became famous, which depends on the opposition of the day; older cases have had longer to reach a verdict; a government opens investigations into its own era's cases less readily than into its predecessor's, so the FIR column measures who held the investigating agencies as much as conduct; and a case that ends without conviction is not thereby proved baseless.
claims.upgradeIf: A complete list of CBI/ED defence-procurement cases by FIR year and stage is obtained (CBI annual reports, Parliament answers)
claims.killIf: The complete list shows the same stage mix under both governments

narratives.claim: Defence and security vendors bought electoral bonds to win orders.
narratives.strongestCase: Documented: the SC-ordered SBI disclosure (ADR match) shows Megha Engineering Rs 966 cr (Rs 584 cr to the BJP); Mahindra & Mahindra (Rs 25 cr) and Cyient (Rs 10 cr) gave only to the BJP; Mahindra's subsidiary holds a documented MoD order (Rs 1,349.95 cr, 27 Aug 2021; PIB) and the parent itself won a MoD light-vehicle contract on 27 Mar 2025, 26 months after its bond, shared with Force Motors (itself a BJP-only buyer of Rs 6.35 cr) (reported). MEIL group company ICOMM Tele Ltd signed a ~Rs 500 cr MoD contract (Buy (Indian), 1,035 radio relay containers) on 15 Jun 2023; MEIL bought BJP bonds on 2023-04-11 and 2023-10-11/12 (company release; The Sentinel; the PIB release was not opened). The three donors with a defence or strategic-works line gave 61.8% of their bonds to the BJP against 47.6% for all donors of Rs 10 cr or more and 46.1% of all matched bonds. The Supreme Court (15 Feb 2024) held there is a 'legitimate possibility' that contributions lead to quid pro quo arrangements. No party or petitioner in the sources makes a defence-specific allegation, so the narrative is weighed as unsupported, not as an alleged claim.
narratives.strongestCounter: No donor in the ADR list is named Tata, L&T, Bharat Forge/Kalyani, Solar Industries, Zen Technologies, Hikvision/Prama or Adani; Megha gave Rs 382 cr to eight other parties and its BJP share (60.5%) is below that of non-defence infrastructure contractors (NCC, Navayuga, APCO, KEC, Kalpataru: 100% each); 29% of all donors gave only to the BJP; the 2021 Mahindra order precedes the bond, and the 2025 order is a competitive Buy (Indian-IDDM) award shared with another maker; the bond buyers and the contract holders differ in two of the cases (M&M parent vs MDS subsidiary in 2021; MEIL vs its group company ICOMM); the Supreme Court (15 Feb 2024) adjudicated no specific donor-order link, and on 2 Aug 2024 dismissed pleas (Common Cause, CPIL) for an SIT into alleged bond quid pro quo, calling the premises 'assumptions at the present stage' (LiveLaw); no award list was matched to bond dates for non-buyers; M&M, MEIL and Cyient were not asked.
narratives.whatWouldChangeThis: A matched series of PIB/DAC awards by vendor and date, run for bond buyers and non-buyers alike, showing a short post-purchase lag only for buyers.

narratives.claim: Bofors was a bribery scandal that the system covered up.
narratives.strongestCase: A CBI FIR (1990) and chargesheet (1999) alleging commissions on the SEK 8,410,660,984 (about Rs 1,437.72 crore) contract of 24 Mar 1986 (CMM order, 4 Mar 2011). Documented handling of the case: the Red Corner Notice against the Italian accused was withdrawn with the Attorney General's approval, the ASG arguing it was 'impinging very heavily upon the exchequer' (CMM order, para 85); the CBI through the Indian Embassy told the Swiss authorities that the documents sent did not connect the McIntyre payments with the Bofors contract (Delhi HC 2005, para 39); the Delhi High Court quashed the corruption charges in 2004 and the Hinduja proceedings in 2005; the CBI's own appeal reached the SC 4,522 days late (Business Standard; Republic); the prosecution of one accused was withdrawn in 2011 (s.321 CrPC). Reported but not opened here: the Dec 2005 request to the UK to release frozen London accounts and the Jan 2011 ITAT finding on payments.
narratives.strongestCounter: Payments to the agents' companies are established in the Swiss documents, but no criminal court found them to be bribes linked to the contract or to a public servant, and no one was convicted; the 2005 judgment found the 14-year, nearly Rs 250 crore investigation produced no case that could proceed; extradition of the Italian accused failed in Malaysia (2002–03) and Argentina (2007), and accused persons died; the ASG's stated rationale for withdrawal was cost and the futility of further extradition attempts (CMM order, paras 85–86); the Supreme Court refused the late appeal (2018, limitation) and the last private appeal (6 Aug 2026). Innocent reading (the platform's own weighing; tier analytic): evidentiary failure across decades, deaths and failed extraditions explain the outcome as well as a cover-up does.
narratives.whatWouldChangeThis: Production in court of the Swiss/Swedish bank evidence the 2005 order found inadequate, or a reopened trial.

narratives.claim: The Tatra/BEML truck purchases involved an alleged Rs 750 crore in bribes and commissions (unattributed figure); CBI sought closure in 2014.
narratives.strongestCase: A CBI FIR on the Defence Minister's directive (2012), the BEML chairman's suspension, an alleged ~60% mark-up through a middleman, and a separate trial in which a charge was framed on 2 Aug 2019 on the alleged Rs 14 crore bribe offer (1,676 HMVs). Rs 750 crore is an unattributed figure in an Oneindia explainer ('It was alleged that BEML officials, and the defence ministry siphoned off at least Rs 750 crore'); no FIR, court or audit document in hand quantifies the loss, and the 2019 charge concerns the bribe-offer case, not the overpricing figure.
narratives.strongestCounter: CBI itself told the court on 26 Aug 2014 that it had insufficient evidence to chargesheet in the BEML case; BEML's then CMD said the General's assessment of the trucks was incorrect and that he would come out clean (The Tribune, 12 Jun 2012); in the bribe-offer case the Defence Minister testified in 2022 that no official complaint had been made to the Ministry and that the Chief had not given documents or recordings (testimony bearing on the bribe-offer case only); the trial outcome is not known.
narratives.whatWouldChangeThis: The trial verdict, or the special court's order on the 2014 closure report (reports say the judge questioned and did not accept it; found only in low-credibility and search-summary sources, so recorded as a gap, not a fact).

narratives.claim: The CAG (Report No. 11 of 2011-12, quoted via secondary sources) described Adarsh as officials subverting rules 'to grab prime government land'; the Bombay HC on 29 Apr 2016 ordered the building demolished for want of a Defence NOC and on security grounds; the SC halted demolition on 22 Jul 2016 by interim order and the appeals remain pending.
narratives.strongestCase: The Bombay High Court (29 Apr 2016: 'Rule is made absolute') ordered demolition and the MoEF ordered it on 14 Jan 2011; the Judicial Commission found 25 of 102 members ineligible and 22 benami transactions; the Army argued no Defence NOC was obtained and that the building threatens the Colaba Military Station. Demolition order documented; the land-grab characterisation is reported (CAG PDF not opened).
narratives.strongestCounter: The Supreme Court halted demolition on 22 Jul 2016 by interim order and the Centre took possession (the Army began the takeover on 30 Jul 2016); the High Court quashed the Governor's sanction to prosecute a former Chief Minister in 2017; the Army's own DEO and HQ MG&G Area recorded in 2000 that the land belonged to the Government of Maharashtra, outside the defence boundary; the Society argues delay and that the Occupation Certificate was revoked without due process; the appeals are unresolved. Symmetry field: the former Chief Minister whose prosecution sanction was quashed joined the BJP in Feb 2024 (reported; not opened here).
narratives.whatWouldChangeThis: The Supreme Court's final judgment on the demolition appeal.

narratives.claim: The Sukna court-martialled generals were guilty of corruption (no conviction survives: AFT acquittal on merits for one; SC voided the other's GCM on composition).
narratives.strongestCase: An Army court of inquiry indicted four generals; two were court-martialled and both GCMs returned guilty findings — one (Jan 2011: loss of seniority, pension service and severe reprimand) and the other (guilty on three charges, dismissal).
narratives.strongestCounter: The AFT on 5 Sep 2014 acquitted the first officer of all charges and held the trial 'influenced and vitiated' (IBTimes); for the second, the AFT (20 Dec 2017) sustained only one charge, unbecoming conduct under s.45, not corruption, and the Supreme Court on 24 Jan 2019 voided the entire GCM because it sat below his rank, without ruling on the merits, noting the surviving charge was 'not of a very serious nature' and declining a fresh GCM.
narratives.whatWouldChangeThis: None available in law for the second officer, since the SC declined remand; for the first, a Union appeal against the AFT order (none found).

narratives.claim: The Government used Pegasus on Indian citizens.
narratives.strongestCase: The Union filed only a 'limited affidavit' and cited national security instead of confirming or denying use; the committee reported the Government did not cooperate; malware was found in 5 of 29 phones; the Court declined in 2025 to release the report. Amnesty International's Security Lab forensically confirmed Pegasus on Indian journalists' phones (2021; and on 28 Dec 2023 for two journalists, the latest infection in Oct 2023) — evidence that Pegasus was used against Indian citizens, not attribution to the Indian state. The New York Times reported on 28 Jan 2022 that India bought Pegasus in 2017 as part of a ~US$2 bn India-Israel package (reported, one outlet; not opened here; denied — see counter).
narratives.strongestCounter: The Technical Committee did not establish Pegasus on any of the 29 phones; the IT Minister's Lok Sabha statement of 19 Jul 2021 (PIB) denies 'illegal surveillance' through the statutory mechanism — it does not deny use of Pegasus as such; the Ministry of Defence told the Rajya Sabha on 9 Aug 2021 that it 'has not had any transaction with NSO Group Technologies' (a documented Parliament answer limited to MoD); the Court itself said possessing spyware is not wrong and the question is against whom it is used. The MEA's 'no information' statement and a minister's response to the NYT report were not opened here.
narratives.whatWouldChangeThis: Publication of the committee report, a forensic attribution of the malware to a state buyer, a sworn Union affidavit confirming or denying procurement or use, or disclosure of procurement records.

narratives.claim: Defence scandals were worse under UPA than under NDA, or the reverse.
narratives.strongestCase: By government at decision and at surfacing: Bofors — decided 1986 (Congress), surfaced 1987, HC quash Feb 2004 under NDA-I; Tatra — purchases from 1986 across governments, surfaced 2012 under UPA; AgustaWestland — contract Feb 2010 (UPA), surfaced 2012–13; Rafale — IGA 2016 (NDA); Adarsh — state Congress-NCP decisions; Sukna — Army, 2008–09; Pegasus — reported 2021. Pegasus, Adarsh and Sukna are not Union defence-procurement decisions. Each side's partisans cite the other's cases.
narratives.strongestCounter: Zero final convictions in all seven named cases; but trial-court convictions exist outside the sample in an NDA-I-era sting case on defence procurement — Tehelka's Operation West End (2001), in which a special CBI court convicted a former Samata Party president and two others on 21 Jul 2020 and sentenced them to four years (not final). The sample is the brief's, not a census; older cases have had longer to resolve; the same fields and tiers apply to every case. Innocent reading (the platform's own weighing; tier analytic): which cases become famous depends on the opposition and the press of the day, so a hand-picked list says nothing about which government had more defence corruption; no comparative metric or census exists either way.
narratives.whatWouldChangeThis: A complete CBI/ED defence-procurement case list by year and stage, and a Parliament answer listing CBI defence-procurement FIRs and MoD debarments by year and stage, run across NDA-I, UPA-I, UPA-II and NDA-II.

The private-vendor-beside-DPSU control was not run for the IADS tender (no bidder list opened). Cases: Bofors beside Rafale and AgustaWestland beside Tatra are run with identical fields (decision date and government; first allegation; investigator; latest stage; counter-record); UPA-era cases (AgustaWestland, Tatra, Sukna, Adarsh) beside NDA-era cases (Rafale, Pegasus) with the same fields: no final conviction in any of the seven records opened, and every alleged claim ships with the other side's recorded answer. Cases are also keyed by the government at first allegation/FIR (c093): FIRs or disciplinary proceedings were opened by the government of the day in 4 of 4 UPA-era cases and 0 of 2 NDA-era cases, a measure of who held the investigating agencies as much as of conduct; outside the seven, the NDA-I-era Tehelka sting produced trial-court convictions in 2020 (not final). Bonds: the infrastructure control (NCC, Navayuga, APCO, KEC, Kalpataru all 100% BJP; Jindal Steel & Power 2.4%) shows the defence-linked donors' 61.8% is not unusual among large contractors.
